data.label: Users accept wrong assistant answers too often
data.description: A quarterly audit of 4,300 escalated support conversations found that in 31% of cases the user acted on an assistant answer that was later shown to be factually wrong. Product wants to know whether surfacing retrieval sources inline reduces that acceptance rate.

data.label: Does an inline source panel reduce acceptance of incorrect answers?
data.description: Shared by both teams. Primary outcome: the proportion of incorrect assistant answers that the user accepts without verification, measured over a 14-day exposure window.
data.scope: Consumer Q&A assistant, English, web client only

data.label: Team A: source panel cuts incorrect-answer acceptance by >= 2 pp
data.description: Pre-registered before any data collection. Directional, with a pre-specified minimum effect of interest so that a small but real effect cannot be re-described afterwards as a large one.
data.null_hypothesis: The source panel has no effect on the acceptance rate of incorrect answers (delta = 0).

data.label: Team A: pre-registered two-arm randomised trial
data.description: Participants randomised 1:1 at first session and held in arm for 14 days. Incorrect answers identified by a blinded adjudication panel that never saw the arm assignment. Analysis plan, exclusions and the single primary outcome were registered before launch.
data.methodology: Two-arm parallel RCT, intention-to-treat, blinded outcome adjudication

data.label: Team A: pre-registration and analysis plan
data.description: Frozen before the first participant was enrolled; the version below is the hash the registry timestamped.

data.label: Team A: trial response dataset (n=1,180)
data.description: One row per adjudicated answer, with arm, acceptance flag, adjudicator id and session timestamp. Checksummed and archived at analysis time.

data.label: Team A: primary analysis code
data.description: Estimates the intention-to-treat difference in acceptance rate.

data.label: Team A: primary pre-registered analysis
data.description: Executed once, on the frozen dataset, against the registered plan. No outcome was inspected before this run.

data.label: Team A: primary outcome, -2.1 pp acceptance
data.description: Acceptance of incorrect answers fell from 34.1% (control) to 32.0% (treatment). Real, small, and only just clear of the pre-specified minimum effect of interest.

statistical_info.multiplicity: single pre-registered primary outcome, no correction needed

data.label: Team A: the source panel reduces wrong-answer acceptance by ~2 pp
data.claim_text: Showing retrieval sources inline reduces acceptance of incorrect assistant answers by 2.1 percentage points (34.1% -> 32.0%, 95% CI [-3.9, -0.3] pp, p = 0.031) over a 14-day exposure window.
data.description: Confidence is deliberately not 0.95: the interval nearly touches zero and the trial covers one client surface only.

data.label: Team A (exploratory): the effect is driven by salience, not by source quality
data.claim_text: The reduction appears to come from the panel's mere presence interrupting the accept reflex, rather than from users reading the cited sources: acceptance fell about as much for sessions where no source link was opened.
data.description: Flagged exploratory in the pre-registration. Subgroup was not randomised and the trial was not powered for it, so the team states 0.45 rather than dressing a hunch as a finding.

data.label: Team A: Team B's effect is confounded by a concurrent model upgrade
data.description: Assistant model v4.2 shipped on 2026-03-26, two days into Team B's window, and independently lowered the error rate. If so, Team B measured the model upgrade, not the panel.
data.null_hypothesis: Adjusting for the model version in effect at each session leaves Team B's estimated effect unchanged.

data.label: Team A: release-window-controlled re-analysis of Team B's extract
data.description: Difference-in-differences on Team B's public log extract, with model version as a time-varying control and the two-day pre-upgrade slice used as the clean comparison.

parameters.control: assistant model version at session time

data.label: Team B's public log extract, re-hosted and checksummed
data.description: The extract Team B published alongside their readout, stored unmodified with a hash so the re-analysis is auditable even though the original source table is gone.

data.label: Team A: difference-in-differences re-analysis code
data.description: Adds the model-version control Team B's read omitted.

data.label: Team A: re-analysis run
data.description: Seeded bootstrap, pinned environment, committed code.

data.label: Team A: Team B's -11.4 pp falls to -1.8 pp once the upgrade is controlled
data.description: Reproducing Team B's uncontrolled comparison recovers their headline almost exactly (-11.2 pp), which rules out a data-handling error. Adding the model-version control collapses it to -1.8 pp, indistinguishable from Team A's own trial estimate and no longer separable from zero.

statistical_info.note: p-value and interval are for the adjusted effect

data.label: Team A: Team B's large effect is a confounded release, not a panel effect
data.claim_text: Team B's -11.4 pp figure is attributable to assistant model v4.2, which shipped two days into their observation window and accounts for -9.1 pp on its own. Controlling for model version leaves -1.8 pp (95% CI [-4.6, 1.0], p = 0.42), consistent with the randomised estimate of -2.1 pp. The panel works; it works about a fifth as well as claimed.
data.description: Cites CLM-B1 directly. Note the cost of that citation: Team B's un-committed run and un-versioned artifact become ancestors of this claim, so its reproducibility and provenance dimensions drop below Team A's own.
